paragraphs: This paper studies how to assess and adapt learned representations when transferring between datasets. Its approach connects machine learning formally with thermodynamics. Rather than evaluating a representation through classification performance alone, it considers several quantities together: rate, distortion, and classification loss. These capture different aspects of the information a model retains and how well that information supports its task.

The authors describe these quantities as lying on a convex equilibrium surface. This geometric description makes it possible to formulate controlled changes to a representation. They prescribe dynamical processes that move along the surface while respecting constraints. One example is an iso-classification process, which trades off rate and distortion while keeping classification loss unchanged.

The paper demonstrates how this process can transfer representations from a source dataset to a target dataset while preserving classification loss. Experiments on standard image-classification datasets validate the theoretical results. The contribution is a framework for reasoning about representation changes through explicit tradeoffs, together with a process that maintains a specified task-related quantity during transfer.
icml-2020-a-free-energy-principle-for-re.tldr: A thermodynamic framework describes how to transfer representations while trading off information-related quantities and keeping classification loss constant.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether the internal responses of a neural network can help predict its ability to generalize beyond its training data. Inspired by cognitive abstraction mechanisms and neuroscience, the authors examine how the complexity of an input relates to the pattern of activations in deeper layers. This provides a way to connect properties of the data with properties of the learned representation.

Their Cognitive Neural Activation metric, or CNA, measures a correlation: input information complexity, expressed through entropy, is compared with the concentration of higher activation values in deeper layers. The metric therefore summarizes a relationship across inputs and network responses. Its purpose is to predict generalization ability from this relationship.

The authors evaluate close to 200 network instances spanning different datasets and architectures. CNA predicts generalization better than the norm- and sharpness-based metrics in that evaluation, particularly with additive noise or corrupted training labels. These empirical findings support CNA as a useful measurement tool and motivate further investigation of how input complexity relates to deeper representations.
icml-2020-abstraction-mechanisms-predict.tldr: A metric linking input complexity to deep-layer activation patterns empirically predicts generalization better than norm- and sharpness-based alternatives.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference often requires approximating a posterior distribution through sampling. Stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics updates a single particle, while ensemble approaches update multiple particles that can interact. Those interactions are intended to make the particles collectively more useful than independent parallel chains. Earlier numerical successes, however, had not established that this advantage holds over a finite run.

The paper proposes an ensemble sampler whose interactions use a non-reversible Markov chain. It then analyzes convergence in a non-asymptotic setting, meaning that the analysis addresses finite progress rather than only eventual behavior. The central result is that interactions can produce faster convergence than independent parallel-chain SGLD if discretization error is appropriately controlled.

That condition is central to the finding: the acceleration depends on managing the error introduced by discrete updates. Numerical experiments show that tuning the interaction can control this error. The paper thus supplies a conditional theoretical explanation for the usefulness of interacting particles, alongside experimental evidence that the required error control can be achieved through interaction tuning.
icml-2020-accelerating-the-diffusion-bas.tldr: Non-reversible particle interactions accelerate ensemble sampling over independent SGLD chains when discretization error is appropriately controlled.

paragraphs: Local search improves a candidate solution through nearby changes, making it a widely used approach to combinatorial optimization. The challenge is to determine how good a solution produced by these local improvements will be relative to the best available solution. This paper develops a framework for answering that question when the objective assigns values to sets.

The key concept is localizability, a property that measures how effective local improvements are for a set function. The authors express approximation guarantees for standard local search algorithms in terms of this property, covering various combinatorial constraints. This creates a common route from a property of the objective to a guarantee about the algorithm's output.

Sparse optimization is the main application. The authors show that restricted strong concavity and restricted smoothness imply localizability, providing sufficient conditions for applying the framework. They also develop accelerated local search algorithms. Experiments in sparse regression and graphical-model structure learning support their practical efficiency, connecting the approximation analysis to problems where selecting a useful sparse structure is central.
icml-2020-approximation-guarantees-of-lo.tldr: Localizability links the effectiveness of local improvements to approximation guarantees and supports accelerated algorithms for sparse optimization.

paragraphs: Deploying generative adversarial networks on mobile devices creates pressure to reduce the computational demands of their generators. Existing compression approaches described in this paper are tied to particular GAN architectures and losses. AutoGAN-Distiller, or AGD, addresses this restriction by applying automated model search to the construction of efficient replacement generators.

AGD begins with a search space designed for efficiency and discovers a generator under specified computational resource constraints. The original GAN guides the search through knowledge distillation, so the compressed model learns from the model it is intended to replace. The framework is automatic and does not require a trained discriminator, making the compression procedure standalone in that specific sense.

The authors evaluate AGD on image translation and super resolution. They report lightweight compressed models that substantially outperform existing alternatives in those evaluations. The approach matters because generator design and compression are handled together: resource constraints shape the search, while distillation supplies guidance from the original model. The framework is presented as applicable across various GAN models.
icml-2020-autogan-distiller-searching-to.tldr: AGD automatically searches for resource-constrained GAN generators using knowledge distillation, without requiring trained discriminators.

paragraphs: An efficient heuristic can produce outputs that violate a monotonic relationship expected of an optimal solution. For example, a parameter may have an intended direction of influence that the approximation fails to respect. This paper studies how to restore such monotonicity using only oracle access to the function, so the correction operates through queries rather than its internal implementation.

The authors give an algorithm that restores monotonicity while reducing the function's expected value by at most epsilon. Its query requirement grows at most logarithmically with the inverse of epsilon but exponentially with the number of parameters. A lower bound shows that the exponential dependence on dimension is necessary for the full restoration problem.

The paper also considers a weaker requirement called k-marginal monotonicity, where every k-dimensional projection must be monotone. For this requirement, the query cost is exponential only in k and polynomial in the total number of parameters. The results expose a tradeoff between the scope of the monotonicity requirement and the cost of enforcing it.
icml-2020-black-box-methods-for-restorin.tldr: Black-box algorithms restore monotonicity with bounded expected-value loss, while a weaker projection-based requirement reduces the dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained, non-convex optimization when gradients are unavailable. Frank-Wolfe methods are useful for constrained problems, but much of the existing work assumes access to first-order information. The authors develop two stochastic zeroth-order variants, which work with function evaluations, and prove faster convergence rates than existing methods for the problems considered.

The first method, FZFW, has function-query complexity O(n^(1/2)d/epsilon^2). The second, FZCGS, improves this to O(n^(1/2)d/epsilon). These expressions describe how the required function queries scale with the quantities appearing in the analysis. The authors relate the results to first-order counterparts, finding an approximate match for FZFW and an improved iteration comparison for FZCGS.

The comparison also reveals that the iteration complexity of the accelerated first-order method NCGS-VR is suboptimal. The authors consequently propose a new algorithm with incremental first-order oracle complexity O(n^(1/2)/epsilon). Benchmark experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution therefore includes both faster methods without direct gradients and an improvement prompted by reexamining the corresponding first-order approach.
icml-2020-can-stochastic-zeroth-order-fr.tldr: Two zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe methods improve convergence guarantees and motivate a faster first-order algorithm for non-convex constrained optimization.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks to recover a reward function from behavior. Deep PQR approaches this problem with deep energy-based policies and a sequence of three estimation steps: first the policy, then the Q-function, and finally the reward. This sequence gives the method its name and organizes reward recovery into connected learning problems.

The framework allows rewards to depend on both the state and the chosen action, and it accommodates stochastic state transitions. Its central assumption is that one anchor action has a known reward. The authors give doing nothing with zero reward as a typical example. This known reference is part of the setup that makes their reward-estimation approach possible.

The theoretical result depends on what is known about the environment. With known transitions, the authors prove that the estimator uniquely recovers the true reward. With unknown transitions, they instead bound its estimation error. Synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate PQR's performance. These results distinguish exact recovery under the stated information conditions from bounded-error estimation when transition information must also be handled.
icml-2020-deep-pqr-solving-inverse-reinf.tldr: Deep PQR estimates policies, Q-functions, and rewards sequentially, using an action with known reward to support identifiable reward recovery.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can be easier to optimize, while practical applications often need compact models. This paper develops a training approach that explores sparse structures while also training an over-parameterized network. It generates a family of models progressing from simple to complex, allowing the search for useful structure to accompany the optimization process.

The method couples two sets of parameters to learn the larger model and structural sparsity in fully connected and convolutional layers simultaneously. Its mathematical foundation uses differential inclusions in inverse scale spaces. A discrete version becomes DessiLBI, an iterative training algorithm. The convergence analysis establishes convergence from any initialization to a critical point of empirical risk; it does not claim convergence to a global optimum.

Experiments across several common network backbones and benchmark datasets find performance comparable to, and sometimes better than, competitive optimizers when exploring structural sparsity. Early stopping also reveals sparse structures in early epochs with test accuracy comparable to fully trained over-parameterized models. These observed winning tickets suggest that useful compact structures can emerge during the initial stages of this training process.
icml-2020-dessilbi-exploring-structural-.tldr: DessiLBI jointly trains large networks and sparse structures, empirically revealing effective sparse subnetworks early in training.

paragraphs: Quantization can make neural-network training more efficient in two ways: compressing activations reduces memory use, and compressing gradients reduces communication costs. Many methods assign values to evenly spaced quantization levels. The paper argues that this uniform treatment can introduce substantial quantization variance and slow convergence in practice.

TinyScript instead applies non-uniform quantization to both activations and gradients. It models their original values using a family of Weibull distributions, then searches for quantization settings that minimize variance. The central idea is to adapt the representation of values to their distribution, so the available bits are used more effectively. The authors also analyze convergence across networks of varying depths and discuss how many bits convergence requires.

In the reported experiments, TinyScript consistently produces lower quantization variance. It achieves model quality comparable to full-precision training while using one to two fewer bits than the uniform quantization counterpart. These findings connect the variance-minimizing design with a practical reduction in numerical precision, while retaining comparable quality in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-dont-waste-your-bits-squeeze-a.tldr: TinyScript adapts activation and gradient quantization to their distributions, retaining comparable model quality with fewer bits in experiments.

paragraphs: Weak supervision builds training labels from noisy sources such as heuristics or crowd workers instead of relying on ground-truth annotations. A central task is estimating how accurate those sources are so their outputs can be combined into probabilistic labels. Existing latent-variable estimation approaches can make this step expensive, with computational costs growing superlinearly in the data.

The authors identify a class of latent-variable models for which the parameters have a closed-form solution. This removes the need for iterative fitting procedures such as stochastic gradient descent. They use the result to build FlyingSquid, a weak-supervision framework that also requires fewer assumptions. Its generalization-error bounds do not require the model to represent the underlying data distribution exactly.

On benchmark weak-supervision datasets, FlyingSquid achieves the same or higher quality than previous approaches and recovers model parameters 170 times faster on average. It also avoids tuning an SGD procedure for that estimation step. The reported speed improvements enable video-analysis and online-learning applications, showing why simplifying label-model estimation can expand where weak supervision is practical.
icml-2020-fast-and-three-rious-speeding-.tldr: FlyingSquid uses closed-form label-model estimation to accelerate weak supervision while maintaining or improving benchmark quality.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes generalization in a synthetic data setting that encompasses several learning problems. These include random-feature learning, neural networks in the lazy-training regime, and the hidden manifold model. Studying them within one framework allows the authors to examine how model size, feature construction, and data correlations relate to prediction performance.

Using the replica method from statistical physics, the authors derive a closed-form expression for asymptotic generalization performance in a high-dimensional regime. The expression covers both under-parameterized and over-parameterized models and a broad choice of generalized linear-model losses. Its scope is therefore an asymptotic analysis of the specified synthetic setting, including both regression and classification.

The framework analytically produces double descent for logistic regression, with a performance peak in error at the interpolation threshold. It also illustrates an advantage of orthogonal projections over random Gaussian projections in random-feature learning and examines correlations in hidden-manifold data. Together, these applications show how a shared theoretical treatment can explain distinct generalization phenomena and provide a basis for extensions to more complex tasks.
icml-2020-generalisation-error-in-learni.tldr: A high-dimensional replica analysis characterizes generalization across random-feature and hidden-manifold models, including logistic-regression double descent.

paragraphs: This paper separates two questions about graph neural networks: which graph properties they can represent, and how their learned predictions generalize. For the first question, it considers models that rely entirely on local information. This includes standard message-passing networks and stronger spatial variants that distinguish neighbors through local orientation or port ordering.

Using a new graph-theoretic formalism, the authors prove that these locally informed models cannot compute several important properties, including shortest or longest cycles, graph diameter, and certain motifs. The result shows that enriching local distinctions does not remove all representational barriers. Its scope is the class of GNNs relying entirely on local information.

For generalization, the paper derives data-dependent bounds for message-passing GNNs. The analysis explicitly incorporates local permutation invariance, the property that local input ordering does not change the relevant computation. These guarantees are much tighter than existing VC-dimension-based bounds and comparable to Rademacher bounds for recurrent neural networks. The two contributions clarify both structural limits on computation and how architectural properties enter generalization analysis.
icml-2020-generalization-and-representat.tldr: The paper proves representational limits for locally informed GNNs and gives tighter, data-dependent generalization bounds for message-passing models.

paragraphs: GAN-generated images can appear realistic enough to be difficult for people to distinguish from photographs. This paper investigates them through frequency representations, which describe image variation at different spatial frequencies. The goal is to identify evidence of generation that may be easier to recognize in this representation than through conventional image-domain inspection.

The authors find pronounced frequency artifacts in GAN-generated images and report that these persist across different architectures, datasets, and resolutions in their analysis. They further trace the artifacts to upsampling operations used in the GAN architectures considered. This links the detectable signal to the image-generation process itself, giving the finding a structural explanation rather than merely cataloging visual irregularities.

Using that analysis, the authors demonstrate automated deep-fake image recognition based on frequency representations. Their method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches in the reported evaluation. The result shows that high perceptual realism can coexist with detectable frequency structure, and that examining how generators build images can provide useful evidence for recognizing their outputs.
icml-2020-leveraging-frequency-analysis-.tldr: Frequency analysis reveals GAN upsampling artifacts and enables automated fake-image recognition that outperforms prior methods in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Training a neural network involves randomness from sources such as data ordering and augmentation. This paper asks whether different realizations of that SGD noise lead to solutions in the same linearly connected region. Linear connectivity provides a way to assess whether training outcomes remain closely related even when the random choices differ.

The authors find that standard vision models become stable to SGD noise early in training. After this point, optimization outcomes are confined to a linearly connected region in the sense studied. They apply the same test to iterative magnitude pruning, the procedure used to identify sparse subnetworks associated with the lottery ticket hypothesis.

In their findings, these subnetworks reach full accuracy only when they are stable to SGD noise. That stability is present at initialization in the small-scale MNIST setting, but emerges early in training for ResNet-50 and Inception-v3 on ImageNet. The results connect the success of the studied sparse subnetworks to training stability and show that the timing of this stability differs across the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-linear-mode-connectivity-and-t.tldr: Pruned subnetworks empirically reach full accuracy only once their training outcomes become stable to SGD noise through linear connectivity.

paragraphs: Online control requires choosing actions while disturbances arrive over time. This paper studies linear-quadratic control with known system dynamics and disturbances that may be chosen adversarially. The objective is to keep regret small: the accumulated cost disadvantage associated with making decisions online. Earlier bounds in this setting grew with the square root of the time horizon unless strong stochastic disturbance assumptions were imposed.

The authors give an algorithm with logarithmic regret for arbitrary adversarial disturbance sequences, provided the state and control costs are known quadratic functions. This changes how the bound grows with the duration of the problem. The improvement retains adversarial disturbances while relying on the stated knowledge and quadratic structure of the control problem.

The method characterizes the optimal offline control law and uses it to reduce control to delayed online learning with approximate advantage functions. Unlike earlier techniques, the analysis does not need to control movement costs between successive iterates. Avoiding that requirement is the key analytical change that enables the logarithmic regret guarantee.
icml-2020-logarithmic-regret-for-adversa.tldr: A reduction to delayed online learning achieves logarithmic regret for known linear-quadratic systems under arbitrary adversarial disturbances.

paragraphs: Generating an unfamiliar combination of familiar attributes is a demanding form of generalization. A model may have encountered the attributes individually without having seen them together. This paper addresses that problem for conditional generative modeling, motivated by the difficulty standard conditional variational autoencoders have in producing attribute combinations absent from training.

The authors extend the conditional VAE with multilinear latent conditioning. This framework represents multiplicative interactions between attributes, changing how attribute information influences the latent representation. The aim is to give the model a structure suited to combining attributes in new ways. The contribution focuses on the conditioning mechanism that guides generation.

The paper implements two variants and demonstrates their effectiveness on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CelebA. These evaluations support the proposed approach for synthesizing unseen attribute combinations. The conditioning framework is presented as usable with any architecture, so its intended role extends beyond one particular model design. Its significance is in making interactions among attributes an explicit part of how a generative model is conditioned.
icml-2020-multilinear-latent-conditionin.tldr: Multilinear latent conditioning models attribute interactions to help conditional generative models synthesize combinations absent from training.

paragraphs: An online learner may combine predictions from experts whose reports are strategic rather than honest. This paper considers experts predicting binary events who want to maximize their influence on the learner. The challenge is to make truthful reporting their best strategy while keeping the learner's regret small relative to the best fixed expert in hindsight.

The authors build algorithms using ideas from wagering mechanisms, which score multiple participants together. For myopic experts, they achieve both incentive compatibility and no regret in full-information and partial-information settings. The qualification about myopic behavior matters: the guarantees address experts focused on immediate incentives rather than strategic effects extending into the future.

Experiments on FiveThirtyEight datasets find regret comparable to classic no-regret algorithms that lack incentive compatibility. The paper also identifies an incentive-compatible algorithm for forward-looking strategic agents, with diminishing regret observed in practice. This latter result is empirical on regret, whereas the myopic setting receives the stated no-regret guarantees. The work connects learning performance with explicit incentives for honest expert reports.
icml-2020-no-regret-and-incentive-compat.tldr: Wagering-based online algorithms combine truthful-reporting incentives with no-regret guarantees for myopic experts.

paragraphs: Online optimization often allows an adversary to choose both the losses a learner faces and their order. This can make sequential learning substantially harder than offline or stochastic alternatives. The paper studies a middle ground: an adversary selects the collection of loss functions, but the learner receives them in uniformly random order.

Under standard well-conditioned-data assumptions, the authors show that ordinary online gradient descent becomes more efficient for two task families. In the first, the cumulative loss is strongly convex even though individual losses may be non-convex. For these tasks, online gradient descent achieves poly-logarithmic regret. The result uses curvature of the cumulative objective rather than requiring convexity of every individual loss.

The second application is online k-PCA. Here, online gradient descent obtains sublinear regret with only a rank-k singular value decomposition per iteration and memory linear in the solution size. Together, the findings show that randomizing presentation order can yield stronger guarantees and efficient computation under the stated data assumptions, even when the collection of losses remains adversarially chosen.
icml-2020-online-convex-optimization-in-.tldr: Uniformly random loss ordering enables stronger regret and efficiency guarantees for online gradient descent under well-conditioned-data assumptions.

paragraphs: Multi-kernel learning chooses a useful kernel from a predefined dictionary for nonlinear function approximation. The dictionary creates a practical tradeoff: including many irrelevant kernels can both hurt accuracy and increase computational cost. This paper develops an online method that actively selects relevant kernels rather than treating the original collection as equally useful throughout learning.

The framework represents feedback from the pruned kernel combination through a graph that is refined as learning proceeds. This graph-based feedback supports the evolving selection process. The authors also use random-feature approximation to make the resulting multi-kernel learning approach scalable. Kernel selection, feedback structure, and approximation therefore form parts of the same online procedure.

The paper proves that the proposed algorithm has sublinear regret, meaning its cumulative regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds. Numerical tests on real datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution addresses the dictionary's influence on both accuracy and complexity through active selection, while providing a theoretical online-learning guarantee for the resulting method.
icml-2020-online-multi-kernel-learning-w.tldr: An online multi-kernel learner actively selects kernels using evolving graph feedback and achieves sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Local graph clustering starts from a seed set and looks for a nearby group of nodes with relatively weak connections to the rest of the graph. This paper develops a family of convex optimization problems based on diffusion through p-norm network flows. The parameter p connects approaches rooted in numerical computation with those rooted in combinatorial flow methods.

The authors characterize optimal solutions and show how they support finding low-conductance cuts around the seeds. At p = 2, the conductance approximation has a quadratic form resembling Cheeger-type spectral guarantees. As p approaches infinity, it becomes a constant-factor approximation resembling max-flow guarantees. Intermediate values provide a smooth transition between these behaviors.

For p at least 2, the proposed optimization problem can be solved in strongly local running time, making locality a computational property as well as a clustering objective. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs compare favorably with existing methods. The framework brings the two methodological traditions together to pursue both speed and robustness to noise.
icml-2020-p-norm-flow-diffusion-for-loca.tldr: A p-norm flow formulation bridges spectral and flow-based local clustering, with smoothly varying approximation guarantees and strongly local computation.

paragraphs: Predicting a group decision requires accounting for how individual participants respond to one another. This paper extends structured prediction by learning parameterized games whose outcomes arise from strategic interaction. The motivation is that a global scoring function alone cannot express individual preferences and asymmetric responses in the way the proposed game model does.

An input context, such as a resolution being voted on, determines initial strategies, player utilities, and interactions. Players repeatedly adjust their strategies to improve their own utilities in response to weighted combinations of others' choices. The prediction is sampled from the resulting equilibrium or near-equilibrium mixed-strategy profile, so uncertainty remains part of the output.

The authors characterize conditions for these updates to converge and for game parameters to be provably recovered from observations. These are conditional results about the model's dynamics and identifiability. On two real voting datasets, the learned games recover interpretable strategic interactions and predict player strategies in new settings. The approach makes interaction among participants an explicit mechanism behind the predicted collective outcome.
icml-2020-predicting-deliberative-outcom.tldr: Learned games predict deliberative outcomes through strategic interaction, with conditional convergence and recovery guarantees and evidence from voting data.

paragraphs: In a stochastic bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses among actions and learns from their rewards. Delayed feedback complicates this process because information about earlier choices may arrive only after further decisions have been made. This paper focuses on cases where different actions have different delay distributions, including distributions with heavy tails.

The authors weaken several assumptions used in earlier delayed-bandit methods, such as uniform delays across actions or restrictive conditions on distribution shape. Their delay assumption requires only a bound on the tail. This still places a condition on how delays behave, while permitting a wider range of action-dependent and heavy-tailed feedback patterns.

To handle this setting, they propose PatientBandits, a simple algorithm based on upper confidence bounds. The analysis supplies both problem-dependent and problem-independent regret bounds, along with performance lower bounds. These results characterize the algorithm's performance from complementary perspectives and provide a theoretical reference for the difficulty of delayed learning. The contribution is to broaden the delay models covered by an efficient bandit approach.
icml-2020-stochastic-bandits-with-arm-de.tldr: PatientBandits handles action-dependent and heavy-tailed feedback delays under a tail-bound assumption, with regret guarantees and performance lower bounds.

paragraphs: Video prediction must account for uncertainty because a sequence of observed frames can have multiple possible futures. Many existing approaches use stochastic recurrent models that predict through the image sequence itself. This paper develops an alternative in which temporal evolution takes place fully in a latent space, separating the dynamics from the process that synthesizes frames.

The proposed stochastic temporal model updates its latent state through a residual rule. Each step modifies the current latent representation, using a first-order scheme motivated by methods for discretizing differential equations. This provides a structured way to describe change over time while retaining stochasticity for uncertain futures. The authors present the model as overcoming design and training difficulties that had hindered this fully latent approach.

On challenging datasets, the model outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods while being simpler and more interpretable according to the authors. The finding supports residual latent dynamics as an effective way to model video evolution. Its significance lies in treating temporal change and image synthesis as separable components within a stochastic prediction model.
icml-2020-stochastic-latent-residual-vid.tldr: A stochastic residual model predicts video dynamics entirely in latent space and outperforms prior methods on challenging datasets.

paragraphs: A relational Markov decision process describes a planning domain with many possible instances, potentially containing different numbers of objects. This paper seeks a neural policy whose parameters can be reused across instances of the same domain. SymNet addresses domains expressed in RDDL, learning shared parameters from a collection of training instances.

For each instance, SymNet constructs a graph and uses relational neural models to compute node embeddings. It scores each concrete action using its first-order action symbol and the embeddings relevant to that action. On a new instance from the same domain, the trained model chooses the highest-scoring action in a single forward pass, without retraining for that instance.

This procedure implicitly represents a generalized policy through shared neural computation. Experiments across nine RDDL domains from IPPC show policies substantially better than random choices. They sometimes also outperform a state-of-the-art deep reactive policy trained from scratch. The findings support transferring a policy across instances within a domain, while the comparison with separately trained policies is explicitly favorable only in some cases.
icml-2020-symbolic-network-generalized-n.tldr: SymNet learns shared relational neural policies that select actions in new instances of the same planning domain without retraining.
